claims.assertion: The GPS track shows an unexempted off-route segment: 09:12–09:26 the driver covered 9.41 km where the optimal route covers 2.05 km, adding 7.35 km and straying up to 1333 m from the optimal route.
The deviation was not agreed in advance: there are no in-app chat messages at all between rider and driver, so nothing shows the rider consented to the change before the segment started.

The driver's claim that flooding and crawling traffic on the Ayer Rajah Expressway justified the detour fails the RD-4 test: the only traffic record near the optimal route is AYE speed band 2 (10–19 km/h) during 08:49–09:12, a band record which under RD-4(b) is corroborative only and not sufficient alone; no traffic incident was recorded near the route during the trip window.

Because this is a RydeTAXI metered trip, the unexempted deviation enters the meter: the total charged was $38.70, of which $25.77 was distance for 18.3 km and $7.56 was time for 29.1 min, and the fare record itself prices the 7.6 km excess at $10.68 ($1.41/km).

Refund on the meter-distance basis of RD-2 is the unexempted segment's extra distance times the trip's per-km rate: 7.35 km × ($25.77 ÷ 18.3 km = $1.41/km) = $10.36; the residual difference against the $10.68 fare-excess figure (0.25 km equivalent) is map-matching residue and is not claimed.
The rider's account shows no upheld prior dispute (0 of 1 in 90 days), so this claim is a first-time, good-faith fare complaint rather than a pattern of claims.
The driver's 90-day history records 2 disputes with 1 upheld, which supports an account-review request, though that profile fact cannot by itself establish the deviation.

weaknesses: The driver will rely on F13 (heavy rain, thundery showers, 18.5 mm) together with F9 (AYE band 2, 10–19 km/h) and his statement F8 to argue a reasonable cause for the reroute; RD-4(b) makes the band evidence corroborative only, but a judge could still treat the combination as an excuse.

The claimed 71% excess (F1: 18.3 km vs 10.7 km) overstates the recoverable amount: RD-2 refunds only the unexempted segment's extra km plus ERP/tolls (which the fare record does not itemise, F6), and the excess above the segment sum (0.25 km, i.e. the difference between F3's 7.35 km and F4's 7.6 km) is expressly non-refundable residue.

what_would_change: Had an LTA incident been recorded on the stretch F3 replaced, before it started, RD-4 would exempt it (−$10.36).
Had the driver carried a prior upheld route dispute in the last 90 days, RD-6 would add an account flag.

claims.assertion: The GPS track shows an unexempted off-route segment: 09:12–09:26 the driver covered 9.41 km where the optimal route covers 2.05 km, adding 7.35 km and straying up to 1333 m from the optimal route.
The deviation was not agreed in advance: there are no in-app chat messages at all between rider and driver, so nothing shows the rider consented to the change before the segment started.

The driver's claim that flooding and crawling traffic on the Ayer Rajah Expressway justified the detour fails the RD-4 test: the only traffic record near the optimal route is AYE speed band 2 (10–19 km/h) during 08:49–09:12, a band record which under RD-4(b) is corroborative only and not sufficient alone; no traffic incident was recorded near the route during the trip window.

Because this is a RydeTAXI metered trip, the unexempted deviation enters the meter: the total charged was $38.70, of which $25.77 was distance for 18.3 km and $7.56 was time for 29.1 min, and the fare record itself prices the 7.6 km excess at $10.68 ($1.41/km).

Refund on the meter-distance basis of RD-2 is the unexempted segment's extra distance times the trip's per-km rate: 7.35 km × ($25.77 ÷ 18.3 km = $1.41/km) = $10.36; the residual difference against the $10.68 fare-excess figure (0.25 km equivalent) is map-matching residue and is not claimed.
The rider's account shows no upheld prior dispute (0 of 1 in 90 days), so this claim is a first-time, good-faith fare complaint rather than a pattern of claims.
The driver's 90-day history records 2 disputes with 1 upheld, which supports an account-review request, though that profile fact cannot by itself establish the deviation.

weaknesses: The driver will rely on F13 (heavy rain, thundery showers, 18.5 mm) together with F9 (AYE band 2, 10–19 km/h) and his statement F8 to argue a reasonable cause for the reroute; RD-4(b) makes the band evidence corroborative only, but a judge could still treat the combination as an excuse.

The claimed 71% excess (F1: 18.3 km vs 10.7 km) overstates the recoverable amount: RD-2 refunds only the unexempted segment's extra km plus ERP/tolls (which the fare record does not itemise, F6), and the excess above the segment sum (0.25 km, i.e. the difference between F3's 7.35 km and F4's 7.6 km) is expressly non-refundable residue.
No in-app chat exists (F7), so there is no rider-side message documenting a refusal of the reroute; the rider must rely on the absence of consent rather than an explicit objection.
The rider's own profile shows 1 dispute filed in 90 days (F14), which the driver may use to characterise the complaint as routine.

claims.assertion: Only one off-route segment exists in the GPS track (F3, 09:12–09:26, +7.35 km), so the entire distance dispute reduces to that single segment and the rider's 18 km vs 11 km framing is not a separate claim.

The 7.35 km extra driven in the disputed segment was a reroute undertaken because the Ayer Rajah Expressway on the optimal route was recorded at speed band 2 (10–19 km/h) across 08:49–09:12, immediately before and during the segment, with heavy rain of 18.5 mm falling at the time (F9, F13), matching my client's statement that the expressway was crawling and flooding (F8).

No traffic incident was recorded near the route during the trip window (F12), so the reroute rests on the congestion band alone, which under the policy is corroborating evidence for the justified-reroute exception rather than a standalone exemption; the segment should therefore be reviewed as a reasonable-cause reroute, not as an unexplained deviation.

The rider never requested or agreed to the reroute — there are no in-app chat messages at all in this trip (F7) — so no segment can be exempted as a passenger-designated stop or agreed route change, and equally the rider's silence carries no evidence that the detour was unexplained.

If any part of the segment is treated as unexempted, the exposure is capped by the fare figures: excess distance billed is $10.68 for 7.6 km at $1.41/km (F4) and the per-km rate derived from the metered fare is $25.77 ÷ 18.3 km = $1.41/km (F6), so the maximum partial refund for the whole of the disputed segment's 7.35 km would be 7.35 × $1.41 = $10.36, not the whole $38.70 the rider appears to seek.

No fee other than metered distance, time and the published platform fee $1.47 was added — waiting fee is $0.00, there was no surge (1.0×) and no manual post-trip add-on (F5, F6) — so there is nothing to refund under the non-metered add-on rules.

My client has 1 upheld dispute in 90 days but 0 upheld route disputes (F15), so the 'repeated route offender' condition for a route-based account flag is not met and no flag_account should attach on route grounds.

weaknesses: The strongest fact against my client is F3: the deviation peaked at 1333 m from the optimal route and drove 9.41 km where the optimal route covers 2.05 km, which the rider will say is far beyond any congestion avoidance and looks like a deliberate detour; F1 (+71% distance) and F2 (+12.6 min) corroborate the scale.

RD-4(a) is not satisfied: F12 records no traffic incident on the optimal route, and under RD-4(b) a speed band of 2 (F9) is only corroborating, so the policy text does not, on its own, exempt the segment on the congestion band alone; bad weather (F13) is not a listed 'reasonable cause' parameter.

The rider will also use RD-5 / RD-3 against my client: F7 shows no chat messages at all, so there was no mutual agreement before leaving the optimal route, and my client's explanation in F8 was given only after the fact.

points.response: Accepted limited to the segment count: F3 shows a single off-route segment, but the disputed amount is still the meter distance it generated, which F6 prices at $25.77 for 18.3 km against a 10.7 km optimal route (F1).

The AYE band 2 record (F9) ends at 09:12, the exact start of the disputed segment in F3, so it covers only the moment of divergence and not the 09:12–09:26 detour; heavy rain (F13) is weather, not a traffic record, and is not an accepted justification under RD-4(a).

The driver's own point is fatal to his defence: RD-4(b) says a speed band record alone does not exempt a segment (it is corroboration only) and RD-4(a) requires a located traffic incident, which F12 confirms does not exist — so under RD-4(c) the segment is handled as an unexempted deviation.

The absence of any chat (F7) means there was no mutual agreement before the driver left the optimal route, which under RD-5 leaves the segment unexempted rather than excused; silence cannot convert an unagreed 1333 m detour (F3) into a consented route.
We agree on the quantum and cite it in our own claim C5: 7.35 km (F3) × $1.41/km derived from F6 = $10.36, and we do not claim the 0.25 km residual between F3's 7.35 km and F4's 7.6 km.

Correct that no add-on fee such as the $5 waiting fee was charged (F5, F6) — our claim is not FARE-1 add-ons but the meter distance units generated by the unexempted segment, which RD-2 refunds for RydeTAXI.
We do not press flag_account on route grounds; F15 shows 0 upheld route disputes, so RD-6's repeated-offender condition is not met and no account flag is requested.

The segment itself is not contested (F3), but RD-1 read with RD-4 does not end at 'deviation exists' — the segment must be reviewed for exemption, and the undisputed record shows the optimal route's expressway (AYE) was at speed band 2, 10–19 km/h, across 08:49–09:12 (F9) while heavy rain of 18.5 mm was falling (F13), which is the reasonable-cause evidence RD-4 contemplates.

I do not dispute the absence of chat (F7), but the rider's point cuts both ways: RD-5 exempts a segment only on the rider's prior consent and, equally, there is no rider message objecting to or refusing the reroute, so F7 cannot convert the absence of agreement into proof that the detour had no reasonable cause.

Conceded in part: F12 records no traffic incident near the optimal route, and under RD-4(b) the AYE band-2 record (F9) is corroborative only, so the band alone cannot formally exempt the segment; this is a ground for human review of the reasonable-cause question, not for treating the rider's $10.36 demand as automatically established.

The arithmetic is admitted — the trip was metered RydeTAXI, total $38.70, distance $25.77 for 18.3 km and time $7.56 for 29.1 min (F6), with the fare record itself pricing 7.6 km of excess at $10.68 (F4) — but RD-2 makes only unexempted segments recoverable, and the segment's exemption question is live.

The $10.36 figure is the correct ceiling if, and only if, the segment is unexempted (7.35 km × $1.41/km, F3, F4, F6); our position is that the segment falls within RD-4's reasonable-cause exception, so the ceiling is not reached and the residual 0.25 km is in any event non-refundable under RD-2.

The rider's own 90-day record of 1 dispute filed with 0 upheld (F14) shows no pattern against the driver and says nothing about this segment's congestion facts (F9, F13); a first-time complaint is not evidence that the reroute lacked reasonable cause.

My client's 90-day record shows 2 disputes with 1 upheld — but that one is a no-show matter and 0 route disputes (F15) — so RD-6's precondition, an upheld route dispute plus this case, is not satisfied and no route-based flag_account attaches.
